$A+B+C=O$

keyPoints: A²=A
B²=B
A²+B²=A+B
modelAnswer: For A², multiply BA=A on the left by A: ABA=A². But AB=B, so ABA=BA=A. Thus A²=A. For B², multiply AB=B on the left by B: BAB=B². Since BA=A, BAB=AB=B. Thus B²=B. Therefore A²+B²=A+B.
stem: If $A$ and $B$ are two matrices such that $A B=B$ and $B A=A$. Find $A^{2}+B^{2}$.

keyPoints: Base case n=1
(AᵏA)ᵀ=Aᵀ(Aᵏ)ᵀ
Induction completes the proof
modelAnswer: Use induction. For n=1, (A¹)ᵀ=Aᵀ. Assume (Aᵏ)ᵀ=(Aᵀ)ᵏ. Then (Aᵏ⁺¹)ᵀ=(AᵏA)ᵀ=Aᵀ(Aᵏ)ᵀ=Aᵀ(Aᵀ)ᵏ=(Aᵀ)ᵏ⁺¹. Hence (Aⁿ)ᵀ=(Aᵀ)ⁿ for every positive integer n.
stem: For any square matrix $A$; prove that $\left(A^{n}\right)^{t}=\left(A^{t}\right)^{n}$.

keyPoints: Y=2X-P
7X=Q+3P
modelAnswer: From 2X-Y=P and X+3Y=Q, substitute Y=2X-P into the second equation: 7X=Q+3P. Thus X=[[1,3,-1],[1,0,3]]. Then Y=2X-P=[[1,0,1],[0,-1,-1]]. Substitution verifies both equations.
stem: Find the matrices $X$ and $Y$ such that $2 X-Y=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 6 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 7\end{array}\right]$ and $X+3 Y=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}4 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 0\end{array}\right]$.

stem: Find the matrices $X$ and $Y$ such that $3 X+Y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}2 & 5 & 3 i \\ 2+7 i & 5 & 7 \\ 2 & 2 & 3 i\end{array}\right]$ and $X+2 Y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 6 & 3 i \\ 7+2 i & 5 i & 7 \\ 3 & 3 & 6\end{array}\right]$

keyPoints: β=-1 from the off-diagonal
α=-9 from the diagonal
modelAnswer: A²=[[7,-1],[-3,12]]. Comparing the (1,2) entry of A²+αI=βA gives -1=β. Then the (1,1) entry gives 7+α=-2, so α=-9. The (2,2) entry checks: 12-9=3=(-1)(-3). Thus α=-9 and β=-1.
stem: If $A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -3\end{array}\right]$ then find $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that, $A^{2}+\alpha I=\beta A$.

keyPoints: X=2J-I
J²=3J
X²=4X+5I
modelAnswer: Let J be the 3×3 all-ones matrix. Then X=2J-I and J²=3J. Hence X²=(2J-I)²=4J²-4J+I=8J+I. Also 4X+5I=4(2J-I)+5I=8J+I. Therefore X²=4X+5I, so X²-4X-5I=O.
stem: If $X=\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1\end{array}\right]$ then prove that $X^{2}-4 X-5 I=0$.

Transpose their sum

aii=0

modelAnswer: Here aji = j²-i² = -(i²-j²) = -aij. Also aii=0. Hence Aᵀ=-A, so A is skew-symmetric.

keyPoints: A zero determinant means singular.
A nonzero determinant means non-singular, including a nonzero complex determinant.
modelAnswer: A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero. Cofactor expansion gives: (i) det=0, so singular. (ii) det=8, so non-singular. (iii) det=5i, so non-singular. (iv) det=−5, so non-singular.

keyPoints: A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero.
Use cofactor expansion and solve the resulting linear equation in λ.
modelAnswer: Set each determinant to zero. (i) det=−23λ+16, so λ=16/23. (ii) det=λ−4, so λ=4. (iii) det=−λ−1+5i, so λ=−1+5i. (iv) det=3+2i−12λ, so λ=(3+2i)/12.

keyPoints: Adding a multiple of one row or column to another does not change a determinant.
Use det(TM)=det(T)det(M) and multilinearity to factor structured determinants.
modelAnswer: (i) Apply determinant-preserving row/column operations (for example R₃←R₃−R₁−R₂) and factor the resulting terms; the determinant reduces to −2(x³+y³). (ii) Successive row and column additions reduce the determinant to (a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²). (iii) If M has rows A,B,C, the left matrix is TM with T=[[n,1,0],[0,n,1],[1,0,n]]. Therefore det(TM)=det(T)det(M)=(n³+1)det(M). (iv) By linearity in column 3, D=det[t,t²,1]+αdet[t,t²,t³]. The first determinant is (x−y)(y−z)(z−x), while factoring xyz from the second gives xyz(x−y)(y−z)(z−x). Hence D=(1+αxyz)(x−y)(y−z)(z−x).
stem:
Using the properties of the determinants prove the following.
(i) $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}x & y & x+y \\ y & x+y & x \\ x+y & x & y\end{array}\right|=-2\left(x^{3}+y^{3}\right)$
(ii) $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & b-c & b+c \\ a+c & b & c-a \\ a-b & a+b & c\end{array}\right|=(a+b+c)\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)$
(iii) $\left|\begin{array}{lll}n a_{1}+b_{1} & n a_{2}+b_{2} & n a_{3}+b_{3} \\ n b_{1}+c_{1} & n b_{2}+c_{2} & n b_{3}+c_{3} \\ n c_{1}+a_{1} & n c_{2}+a_{2} & n c_{3}+a_{3}\end{array}\right|=\left(n^{3}+1\right)\left|\begin{array}{lll}a_{1} & a_{2} & a_{3} \\ b_{1} & b_{2} & b_{3} \\ c_{1} & c_{2} & c_{3}\end{array}\right|$
(iv) $\left|\begin{array}{lll}x & x^{2} & 1+\alpha x^{3} \\ y & y^{2} & 1+\alpha y^{3} \\ z & z^{2} & 1+\alpha z^{3}\end{array}\right|=(1+\alpha x y z)(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$

keyPoints: A homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution only when the coefficient matrix is singular.
Use elimination to express the dependent variables in terms of a free parameter.
modelAnswer: Gaussian elimination gives: (i) x₂=2x₃ and x₁=x₃, so (x₁,x₂,x₃)=t(1,2,1), t≠0. (ii) x₃=5x₂/2 and x₁=−7x₂/2, so (x₁,x₂,x₃)=t(−7,2,5), t≠0. (iii) x₂=2x₃ and x₁=x₃, so (x₁,x₂,x₃)=t(1,2,1), t≠0. (iv) the coefficient determinant is −73≠0, so only the trivial solution (0,0,0) exists.

keyPoints: Choose an invertible coding matrix so decoding by its inverse is possible.
Pad words with X to complete pairs or triples.
modelAnswer: Use A=1,…,Z=26 and X as padding. For pairs, take K₂=[[1,1],[1,2]], K₂⁻¹=[[2,−1],[−1,1]]. K₂ encodes PAKISTAN as (17,18),(20,29),(39,59),(15,29); ISLAMABAD as (28,47),(13,14),(14,15),(3,4),(28,52); and COLLEGE as (18,33),(24,36),(12,19),(29,53). Applying K₂⁻¹ decodes them (discard padding X). For triples, take K₃=[[1,1,0],[0,1,1],[0,0,1]], K₃⁻¹=[[1,−1,1],[0,1,−1],[0,0,1]]. K₃ encodes PAKISTANX as (17,12,11),(28,29,20),(15,38,24); ISLAMABAD as (28,31,12),(14,14,1),(3,5,4); and COLLEGEXX as (18,27,12),(17,12,7),(29,48,24). Applying K₃⁻¹ recovers the original letters.

keyPoints: A translation 5 units below maps y to y−5.
Use the inverse coordinate substitution y=y′+5 in the original equation.
modelAnswer: For a downward translation by 5, use homogeneous coordinates: T=[[1,0,0],[0,1,−5],[0,0,1]], so (x′,y′,1)ᵀ=T(x,y,1)ᵀ. Thus x=x′ and y=y′+5. Substituting in x²+y²−9=0 gives x′²+(y′+5)²−9=0.
stem: Write the transformation matrix and the transformed equation of the curve $x^{2}+y^{2}-9=0$ when it is moved 5 units below.

keyPoints: A left translation maps x′=x−2.
Substitute x=x′+2 into the original equation.
modelAnswer: For a translation 2 units left, T=[[1,0,−2],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]], so x=x′+2 and y=y′. Substitute into x²+4x−3y=8: x′²+8x′−3y′=−4.
stem: Write the transformation matrix and the transformed equation of the curve $x^{2}+4 x-3 y=$ 8 when it is moved to 2 units on the left.

keyPoints: A right translation maps x′=x+1.
